foods.name: Blue cheese
foods.why: Blue cheese is a soft, moist cheese, which is exactly the room listeria likes. Cold on a cheese board it is a no for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Melted into a sauce or cooked in a dish and served properly hot, blue cheese is fine.
foods.swap: A sharp aged cheddar or a shave of pecorino gives you the same salty hit.

foods.name: Brie and camembert
foods.why: Brie careful: soft white-mould cheeses hold moisture, and listeria likes that. Cold from the board they are benched for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked right through and served bubbling hot, baked brie and camembert are back on the menu.
foods.swap: Build the board from hard cheeses instead: cheddar, gouda, parmesan, a bit of quince paste.

foods.name: Cheese
foods.why: Depends which cheese, and whether it's hot:

variants.label: Hard cheese
variants.why: Cheddar, tasty, parmesan, gouda, edam, Swiss and pecorino are too dry and salty for listeria to throw a party in. Grate news.

variants.label: Soft cheese, uncooked
variants.why: Brie, camembert, blue, feta, ricotta, burrata, bocconcini and soft goat cheese are moist and low-acid, which is listeria's favourite postcode.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook it right through and eat it while it is still bubbling hot: baked brie, lasagne, spanakopita.
variants.swap: A cheddar, parmesan and cherry tomato board scratches exactly the same itch.

variants.label: Cream cheese and cottage cheese
variants.why: Pasteurised and sealed, so these two are fine. Keep them in the fridge and eat within two days of opening.

variants.label: Soft cheese in a hot cooked dish
variants.why: Heat sorts it out. Melted mozzarella on pizza, ricotta baked into a lasagne, feta in a hot spanakopita: all back on the menu, served steaming.

variants.label: Unpasteurised or raw-milk cheese
variants.why: Raw-milk cheese skips pasteurisation, the step that deals with listeria and salmonella in the first place.
variants.swap: Any pasteurised hard cheese, which is very nearly everything in the supermarket fridge.

foods.name: Cheese spread
foods.why: Pasteurised and shelf stable until you open it, so spread it on thick. Into the fridge after opening and follow the label.

foods.name: Cottage cheese
foods.why: Pasteurised and fine, protein and all. Keep it in the fridge with the lid on and finish it within a couple of days of opening.

foods.name: Cream and butter
foods.why: Pasteurised cream and butter are a straight yes: whipped, thickened, soured or spread thick on hot toast. Normal fridge rules apply.

foods.name: Cream cheese
foods.why: Pasteurised, so it is a yes on your bagel. Keep it cold and finish it within about 2 days of opening, same as any fresh dairy.

foods.name: Custard
foods.why: Shop-bought custard is pasteurised and ready to pour. Eat it freshly opened, keep it in the fridge and use it within a day.

foods.name: Feta and ricotta
foods.why: Soft cheeses can carry listeria when they are eaten cold. Baked into something hot, they are completely back on the menu.
foods.makeItGreen: Baked through a hot dish: spanakopita, lasagne, a ricotta pasta bake, served steaming.
foods.swap: Crumble hard cheese over the salad, or go for cottage cheese or cream cheese from the fridge.

foods.name: Fresh mozzarella, burrata and bocconcini
foods.why: These fresh cheeses are soft and full of moisture, and that is where listeria settles. Eaten cold and uncooked they are out for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked right through to 75 degrees and eaten hot, on a pizza or baked in a dish, it is a yes.
foods.swap: Melted mozzarella on a hot pizza, or shaved hard cheese over the tomatoes and basil.

foods.name: Fried ice cream
foods.why: The batter is usually egg based and the fry is quick on purpose, to keep the middle frozen. That means the egg may never cook through.
foods.swap: Tub ice cream under a hot chocolate sauce, or a warm baked pudding with a scoop on the side.

foods.name: Haloumi
foods.why: Cooked until it squeaks and served hot is exactly the safe way with haloumi. Grill it or pan fry it rather than eating it cold from the pack.

foods.name: Hard cheeses
foods.why: Hard cheese is too dry and salty for listeria to throw a party in. Cheddar, parmesan and the whole firm crew are a straight yes.

foods.name: Ice cream from a tub
foods.why: Tub and packaged ice cream is pasteurised and sealed, so it is a yes. The tub is the trick: it is soft serve from a machine that is the problem.

foods.name: Melted mozzarella
foods.why: Bubbling on a pizza or baked right through a dish, the heat has done the work for you. Melted mozzarella is a green light.

foods.name: Milk
foods.why: Depends whether it's pasteurised:

variants.label: Pasteurised, including UHT
variants.why: Everything in the supermarket fridge and on the long-life shelf is pasteurised, and that is the step that sorts out the bacteria. Buttermilk counts too.

variants.label: Raw or unpasteurised, including bath milk
variants.why: Raw milk skips pasteurisation, so listeria, salmonella and E. coli can survive in it. Bath milk is raw milk with a label workaround.
variants.swap: Any regular supermarket milk, dairy or plant based. Same white, none of the worry.

variants.label: Soy, oat, almond and other plant milks
variants.why: Commercially made plant milks are heat treated in the carton, so the whole aisle is yours. Soy products in general are a yes.

foods.name: Milkshake made at home
foods.why: Pasteurised milk, tub ice cream and your own clean blender: you control the hygiene end to end, so blend away.

foods.name: Paneer
foods.why: Paneer is made from pasteurised milk and it almost always turns up cooked and hot. Two ticks in the one curry.

foods.name: Pasteurised milk
foods.why: Pasteurisation is the whole point: it has already been heat treated for you. Fridge milk or long life off the shelf, both a yes.

foods.name: Processed cheese slices
foods.why: Pasteurised and sealed, so slices are good to go. Once the pack is open, keep it in the fridge and eat it within a couple of days.

foods.name: Scooped gelato
foods.why: Gelato is scooped from tubs, so the risk sits well below soft serve. The unknown is the shared scoop and the bench it rests on.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for a fresh scoop from a covered tub, or take a sealed tub home from the freezer aisle.
foods.swap: Tub ice cream at home, or a frozen-banana nice cream.

split.note: The sheets never actually rule on scooped gelato, so this one is a judgement call. Here is both sides, in the open.

positions.label: The source sheets
positions.says: Ice cream from a tub is green, and machine soft serve is red because the dispenser can harbour listeria. Scooped gelato sits between the two, and none of our sheets names it.

positions.label: Our call
positions.says: Yellow. The tub keeps the risk low, but the shared scoop and the bench it rests on are unknowns, so we hedge rather than wave it fully green.

foods.name: Soft goat cheese
foods.why: Soft goat cheese is moist and mould ripened, so it sits with brie and feta on the not-right-now list while it is cold.
foods.makeItGreen: Baked or grilled until it is hot right through, like a warm goat cheese tart, and it is back on.
foods.swap: A hard goat gouda, or aged cheddar crumbled over the beetroot salad.

foods.name: Soft serve ice cream
foods.why: It is not the ice cream, it is the machine. Soft serve dispensers are fiddly to clean and listeria can settle inside them.
foods.swap: A scoop from a sealed tub at home, or frozen-banana nice cream in a cone.

foods.name: Thickshakes and McFlurry
foods.why: Same story as soft serve: these all come out of a dispensing machine that is tricky to clean, and listeria can hide in the works.
foods.swap: Blend your own thick shake at home with tub ice cream and cold milk.

foods.name: Unpasteurised milk and raw-milk cheese
foods.why: With no pasteurisation there is nothing standing between you and listeria, salmonella or E. coli. This one is a firm no for now.
foods.makeItGreen: The pasteurised version of the very same thing is a green light.
foods.swap: Pasteurised milk, and cheese made from pasteurised milk: cheddar, gouda, parmesan.

foods.name: Yoghurt
foods.why: Every pasteurised kind is a yes, live cultures included. Greek, natural, flavoured or pot set: pick your favourite and dig in.

foods.name: Emmental
foods.why: Emmental is the original Swiss cheese, holes and all, and Swiss sits on the hard cheese green list: too dry for listeria to set up in. Stack the toastie high.

foods.name: Jarlsberg
foods.why: Jarlsberg is a Swiss-style firm cheese, and the hard cheese rule is really about dryness: nowhere for listeria to party. The sweet, nutty slices are all yours.

foods.name: Provolone
foods.why: Provolone is aged until it is firm and dry, which puts it with cheddar and friends on the hard cheese green list. Listeria cannot get a party started in there.

foods.name: Manchego
foods.why: Manchego is a hard, aged sheep's milk cheese, and hard is the magic word: too dry for listeria. The Spanish corner of the cheese board stays open.

foods.name: Red Leicester
foods.why: Red Leicester is a firm cheddar cousin with a sunset colour, and it plays by the same hard cheese rule: too dry for listeria. Slice away.

foods.name: Double Gloucester
foods.why: Double Gloucester is a firm British classic from the cheddar school: hard, dry and no room for listeria. A yes on crackers or melted over toast.

foods.name: Raclette
foods.why: Depends how it's served:

variants.label: Melted until bubbling
variants.why: Raclette's whole job is being melted until it bubbles, and served hot like that it is a green light, raw-milk wheel or not. Heat settles it.

variants.label: Cold wedge from the board
variants.why: Cold raclette is a moist semi-soft cheese, often made from raw milk, so it sits with havarti on the bench until bub arrives.
variants.makeItGreen: Under the grill or over potatoes until it bubbles, and it is straight back on.
variants.swap: A firm pasteurised alpine cheese like gruyere from the green list.

foods.name: Hard goat cheese
foods.why: Goat cheese firms up as it ages, and once it is hard and dry the door shuts on listeria, same as cheddar. It is the soft, spreadable goat cheese that waits for now.

foods.name: Havarti
foods.why: Havarti keeps more moisture than its hard cheese cousins, and moisture is what listeria likes, so cold slices are benched for now. Annoying, but easy to fix.
foods.makeItGreen: Melted until bubbling in a toastie or on a burger, havarti is back on.
foods.swap: Gouda or edam scratch the same creamy, mild itch from the green list.

foods.name: Stracchino
foods.why: Stracchino, also sold as crescenza, is a young, spreadable soft cheese, and soft plus moist is exactly where listeria likes to lurk. One for after bub arrives.
foods.makeItGreen: Baked through something hot, like a cheesy focaccia straight from a hot oven, it is a yes.
foods.swap: A smear of cream cheese from the fridge gets you most of the way there.

foods.name: Taleggio
foods.why: Taleggio is a soft washed-rind cheese, moist right through, so the soft cheese rule parks it for now. The fridge will keep smelling of it, as a memento.
foods.makeItGreen: Melted into a hot dish, think baked polenta or a gnocchi bake, served steaming, and it is back.
foods.swap: For a big savoury hit served cold, go a proper aged cheddar or a shave of parmesan.

foods.name: Mascarpone
foods.why: Mascarpone is pasteurised cream in cheese clothing, so like cream cheese it is a yes. Keep it cold and use it within a couple of days. The tiramisu problem is the raw egg, never the mascarpone.

foods.name: Labneh
foods.why: Labneh is yoghurt, strained until it thinks it is cheese, and every pasteurised yoghurt is a yes. Make it at home or buy a sealed tub, and give the open deli bowl a miss.

foods.name: Quark
foods.why: Quark is a fresh pasteurised dairy in the cottage cheese family, so it is a green light. Fridge rules apply: lid on, eaten within a couple of days of opening.

foods.name: Skyr
foods.why: Skyr is Iceland's extra-thick style of yoghurt, made from pasteurised milk, and every pasteurised yoghurt is a yes. Protein-packed bonus, no catch.

foods.name: Kefir yoghurt
foods.why: The thick, spoonable kefir yoghurt in the fridge aisle is made from pasteurised milk, so the yoghurt rule says yes. It is the fizzy bottled kefir drink that stays on the red list with kombucha.

foods.name: Yoghurt drinks
foods.why: Drinking yoghurt and the little probiotic bottles like Yakult start with pasteurised milk, and pasteurised yoghurt in any form is a yes. Sip away.

foods.name: Fromage frais
foods.why: Fromage frais is fresh pasteurised dairy sitting halfway between yoghurt and cream cheese, so it is a yes. That includes the kids' pouches you are definitely allowed to steal.

foods.name: Custard tart
foods.why: A baked custard tart is cooked custard in cooked pastry, and baked means the eggs are sorted. Old-school nutmeg number or a Portuguese tart with the scorched top, both a yes.

foods.name: Evaporated milk
foods.why: Evaporated milk is sealed in the can and heat treated on the way in, so it is a yes. Once opened, treat it like fresh milk: fridge, covered, used within a couple of days.

foods.name: Condensed milk
foods.why: Sweetened condensed milk is canned and heat treated, and all that sugar makes it very unfriendly real estate for bacteria. The spoon straight from the tin is between you and the tin.

foods.name: Creamed rice
foods.why: Canned creamed rice follows the canned food rule: sealed and heat treated, so it is a yes. Fridge it once opened and eat it within a day or two, if it lasts that long.

foods.name: Flavoured milk
foods.why: Flavoured milk is pasteurised milk with a party trick, so it is a yes. Coffee and choccy flavours count a little toward the day's 200mg caffeine budget, strawberry does not.

foods.name: Frozen yoghurt in a tub
foods.why: From a supermarket tub, frozen yoghurt follows the tub ice cream rule: pasteurised, sealed, no dodgy machine involved. The swirly machine froyo at the shops is the red one.

foods.name: Shredded cheese
foods.why: Depends what got shredded, and where it is headed:

variants.label: Shredded cheddar, tasty or parmesan
variants.why: Hard cheese stays hard cheese after the grater: too dry for listeria. Sprinkle from the bag with a clear conscience, then reseal it and back in the fridge.

variants.label: Shredded mozzarella or pizza blend, cold from the bag
variants.why: The fact sheets sort cheese by moisture, and bagged mozzarella sits in the middle, so the stricter reading says no cold handfuls while you cook.
variants.makeItGreen: Melt it. Bubbling on a pizza or toastie is exactly what that bag was born for.
variants.swap: Keep a bag of shredded tasty next to it for the cold sprinkling.

variants.label: Melted on anything
variants.why: Once it is bubbling over the pizza, jaffle or nachos, the heat has done the work, whatever the blend.

foods.name: Bacon, served hot
foods.why: Cooked in the pan and served hot, bacon is a yes. Heat is what handles any listeria, so eat it straight off the heat rather than cold from the fridge.

foods.name: Beef, lamb, pork and chicken, cooked through
foods.why: Cooked right through with no pink and clear juices, meat is a green light and a top iron hit. Get leftovers into the fridge fast, then reheat them steaming hot within a day.

foods.name: Canned or jar meat and fish paste
foods.why: Shelf-stable tins and jars are safe as houses until you open them. After that, treat it like any fresh food: straight into the fridge and eaten up quickly.

foods.name: Cold deli meats
foods.why: Cold cured and cooked meats can carry listeria, and freshly sliced is not safer: the slicer itself can spread it around. Heat is what changes the answer.
foods.makeItGreen: Heat it until it is steaming hot right through, like on a pizza or in a toastie, and it is back on.
foods.swap: Tinned tuna, hot roast chicken, or firm-cooked egg in the sanga.

foods.name: Cold leftover BBQ chicken
foods.why: Once cooked chicken has gone cold, listeria gets its chance. Straight from the fridge is a no, but it is only a reheat away from a yes.
foods.makeItGreen: Reheat it until it is steaming hot right through, and finish it within a day of buying it.
foods.swap: Hot chook fresh from the shop, or reheated chicken piled into a wrap.

foods.name: Cold meats and chicken from sandwich shops and cafes
foods.why: Cold chicken and cold cuts at a sanga shop sit in the fridge and share a slicer and tongs, which is listeria's happy place.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for it toasted until the filling is steaming hot right through.
foods.swap: A hot toasted sanga, or a salad you watched them make fresh.

foods.name: Ham
foods.why: Depends whether it's hot or cold:

variants.label: Heated until steaming hot
variants.why: On a pizza or in a toastie, ham gets its full redemption arc. Listeria gives up at 74 degrees held for 2 minutes, and a hot toastie sails past that.

variants.label: Cold, from the pack or deli counter
variants.why: Cold ready-to-eat deli meat is the classic listeria risk, and freshly sliced is not safer: the slicer itself is the problem.
variants.makeItGreen: Heat it until it is properly steaming, then it is all yours.
variants.swap: A hot ham and cheese toastie, or tinned tuna with jar mayo in the sanga instead.

variants.label: Cold cuts on a Chrissy platter
variants.why: Platter ham has usually been out of the fridge a while and handled by half the family, so the risk stacks up.
variants.makeItGreen: Take your slices to the pan first and fry them until they are steaming, then load up your plate.
variants.swap: Hot glazed ham straight out of the oven, before it hits the platter.

foods.name: Ham or salami, heated steaming hot
foods.why: Heat is the loophole. Deli meats taken right up to steaming hot, on a pizza or in a toastie, are back on the menu: listeria does not survive 74C for two minutes.

foods.name: Hot BBQ chicken, fresh from the shop
foods.why: Straight from the hot cabinet and still steaming, BBQ chook is a green light. Leftovers go into the fridge within 2 hours and get eaten within a day, reheated hot.

foods.name: Jerky and biltong
foods.why: Jerky and biltong are dried and cured but never cooked, so nothing in there has been through heat. Sitting this one out for now.
foods.swap: Salted nuts, roasted chickpeas, or hot cooked meat straight off the barbie.

split.note: No sheet actually names jerky or biltong, so this is a judgement call, and stricter wins. Here is both sides.

positions.label: The source sheets
positions.says: None of our pregnancy sheets lists jerky or biltong. The nearest rule is the cold cured meat one: listeria risk, fixed only by heating until steaming hot.

positions.label: Our call
positions.says: Red. It is dried and cured but never cooked, and there is no sensible way to serve jerky steaming hot, so the stricter reading of the cured meat rule wins.

foods.name: Liver
foods.why: Liver is an iron legend, but it is packed with retinol and too much vitamin A is not great for the bump. Keep it to 50g a week, about one small slice.
foods.makeItGreen: Stay under 50g a week, roughly one small slice, and cook it right through.
foods.swap: Red meat, chickpeas or leafy greens bring the iron with no vitamin A cap.

foods.name: Pâté (refrigerated)
foods.why: Refrigerated pâté is a double whammy: listeria from a chilled ready-to-eat spread, plus a big hit of vitamin A from the liver.
foods.swap: Shelf-stable tinned or jar pâté (into the fridge once opened), or a home-made white bean dip.

foods.name: Prosciutto
foods.why: Cured but never actually cooked, so cold prosciutto can carry listeria. Freshly sliced is not safer either, the slicer can pass it along.
foods.makeItGreen: Crisp it in a hot pan or under the grill until it sizzles, then scatter it over pasta or pizza.
foods.swap: Hot crispy prosciutto shards over pasta, or hot roast chicken in a sanga.

foods.name: Rare or medium-rare steak
foods.why: Pink in the middle can carry toxoplasmosis, so this one waits. The good news: a well-done steak is still very much a steak.
foods.makeItGreen: Order it well done, cooked right through with no pink left, and it is a green light.
foods.swap: A well-done scotch fillet with all the trimmings.

foods.name: Raw mince dishes (tartare, kibbeh)
foods.why: Raw mince has never met heat, so nothing has knocked out the bugs. Tartare and kibbeh are benched for the next few months.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook the mince right through until it is steaming: same flavours, safe version.
foods.swap: A rich slow-cooked bolognese, or a burger patty cooked all the way through.

foods.name: Sausages, cooked through
foods.why: Cook a snag right through until there is no pink left and it is a green light. The Bunnings sausage sizzle lives to see another Saturday.

foods.name: Steak, well done
foods.why: No pink for now, but a steak cooked all the way through is all yours. Well done still comes with chips, and the iron is doing you both a favour.

foods.name: Veggie pâté (refrigerated)
foods.why: The refrigerated pâté rule is about the fridge, not the meat. Chilled ready-to-eat spreads can carry listeria, the veggie ones included.
foods.swap: A home-made white bean or beetroot dip, or a shelf-stable jar version.

foods.name: Mortadella, cold from the deli
foods.why: Mortadella is cooked at the factory, but it is sliced and eaten cold, and cold deli meat is listeria's favourite hangout. The deli slicer can pass it along too.
foods.makeItGreen: Steaming hot on a pizza or grilled into a toasted focaccia, mortadella is back on the menu.
foods.swap: A hot ham and cheese toastie, fresh off the press.

foods.name: Pastrami, cold from the deli
foods.why: Pastrami gets smoked and steamed, but by the time it is sliced at the deli it is a cold ready-to-eat meat, and that is listeria territory. Heat flips the answer.
foods.makeItGreen: Order the reuben: pastrami grilled until it is steaming hot right through is a green light.
foods.swap: Hot roast beef, carved thick and served steaming.

foods.name: Pepperoni, cold from the cabinet
foods.why: Pepperoni is cured and fermented, never cooked, so cold slices from the deli cabinet carry the usual listeria risk. Its true home fixes everything.
foods.makeItGreen: On a pizza out of a screaming hot oven, pepperoni is completely fine. The oven does the work.
foods.swap: A fresh, blistering hot pepperoni pizza.

foods.name: Chorizo
foods.why: Depends whether it's sizzling or straight off the deli board:

variants.label: Cooked hot in the pan or paella
variants.why: Fried until it sizzles or simmered through a paella and served hot, chorizo is a green light. Fresh raw chorizo just needs cooking right through like any snag.

variants.label: Cured, eaten cold
variants.why: Cured chorizo eaten cold off the board is ready-to-eat deli meat, which is exactly where listeria likes to lurk.
variants.makeItGreen: Slice it into a hot pan and fry until it sizzles, then it is all yours.
variants.swap: Hot chorizo with eggs cooked firm.

foods.name: Kabana
foods.why: Kabana is a cured, ready-to-eat sausage that never sees heat, so it sits in the cold deli meat basket with the listeria risk. The party platter can spare it.
foods.makeItGreen: Sliced over a pizza and baked until it sizzles, kabana counts as properly heated through.
foods.swap: Cheddar cubes and crackers hold the platter together just fine.

foods.name: Twiggy sticks
foods.why: Twiggy sticks and mettwurst are cured and dried but never cooked, so the cold deli meat rule applies. One for the after-baby snack drawer.
foods.swap: Salted nuts, pretzels or crunchy roasted chickpeas for the road trip slot.

foods.name: Bresaola
foods.why: Bresaola is beef cured by salt, air and patience rather than heat, so it counts as raw cured meat with the usual listeria risk. Months, not forever.
foods.swap: Hot roast beef sliced thin, or prosciutto crisped in a hot pan until it shatters.

foods.name: Speck
foods.why: Speck is smoked, but it is a cold-smoke and cure job rather than actual cooking, so straight off the board it counts as cold deli meat.
foods.makeItGreen: Diced and fried until it sizzles into a hot dish, speck is a green light, same trick as bacon.
foods.swap: Crispy bacon, hot out of the pan.

foods.name: Pancetta
foods.why: Depends whether it's crisped or cold:

variants.label: Crisped in a hot pan
variants.why: Fried until it shatters or cooked through a hot pasta, pancetta is a green light. Crisped hot, it is basically fancy bacon, and bacon rules apply.

variants.label: Cold, straight off the slicer
variants.why: Cured but never cooked, cold pancetta is classic listeria territory, and the deli slicer does not help.
variants.makeItGreen: Into the hot pan until it is properly sizzling, then it is back on the menu.
variants.swap: Crispy bacon, or hot crisped prosciutto shards.

foods.name: Devon, fritz and polony
foods.why: Devon, fritz, polony: one sausage, many names, same rule. It is a cold ready-to-eat deli meat, so the listeria caution applies for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Fried in a hot pan until the edges curl and it is steaming, old-school devon and sauce style.
foods.swap: A toasted cheese and Vegemite sanga for the school-lunch nostalgia hit.

foods.name: Turkey
foods.why: Depends whether it's roasted or from the deli:

variants.label: Roast turkey, hot from the oven
variants.why: Cooked right through with clear juices and served hot, roast turkey is a green light. Bake the stuffing in its own dish though, not inside the bird.

variants.label: Deli turkey slices, cold
variants.why: Cold sliced turkey is deli meat like ham, so the listeria rule applies, and freshly sliced is not any safer.
variants.makeItGreen: Toast it until the filling is steaming hot right through.
variants.swap: Hot roast turkey, or a toasted turkey and cheese melt.

foods.name: Schnitzel, cooked through
foods.why: Crumbed, fried and cooked right through with no pink in the middle, a schnitzel is a green light, chicken, pork or veal. Served hot with lemon, it is doing everything right.

foods.name: Rissoles, cooked through
foods.why: Mince has to be cooked right through, and a rissole flattened on the barbie until the juices run clear is exactly that. Green light, tomato sauce strongly encouraged.

foods.name: Meatballs, cooked through
foods.why: Simmered through a bubbling sugo or baked until cooked right through, meatballs are a green light, kofta included. No pink in the middle is the only rule.

foods.name: Pulled pork, served steaming hot
foods.why: Hours in the slow cooker or smoker takes pork well past cooked through, and served steaming hot it is a green light. Fridge any leftovers fast and reheat them steaming.

foods.name: Ribs, hot off the grill
foods.why: Cooked low and slow until the meat gives up the bone, then served hot, ribs are a green light. Get sticky to the elbows, you have earned it.

foods.name: Chicken wings, cooked through
foods.why: Cooked right through with no pink at the bone and served hot, chicken wings are all yours. If a joint still looks pink inside, send it back for more time.

foods.name: Slow-cooked brisket, served hot
foods.why: Half a day in the smoker or slow cooker is about as cooked as meat gets. Served hot and fresh off the board, brisket is a green light; cold leftovers just need a steaming reheat.

foods.name: Dim sims, steaming hot
foods.why: Straight from the steamer or the fryer and almost too hot to hold, a dimmy is a green light. Skip any that have been sitting around lukewarm in the warmer.

foods.name: Spring rolls, fried hot
foods.why: Deep-fried until the filling is piping hot right through, spring rolls are a green light, the mighty Chiko included. Fresh and hot is the whole trick.

foods.name: Duck
foods.why: Depends how pink the kitchen likes it:

variants.label: Cooked right through
variants.why: Roast duck, Peking duck or a well-done breast, cooked through with no pink and served hot, follows the same happy rule as any other poultry: green light.

variants.label: Duck breast served pink
variants.why: Restaurants love duck breast blushing pink, but pink meat carries the same toxoplasmosis risk as a rare steak.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask for it cooked right through with no pink left. The crispy skin survives just fine.
variants.swap: Crispy-skin roast duck or duck pancakes, hot from the kitchen.

foods.name: Venison and game, cooked through
foods.why: Venison, rabbit, quail and their mates follow the same rule as beef and lamb: cooked right through with no pink, served hot, green light. Game is lean and iron-rich, so enjoy.

foods.name: Kangaroo
foods.why: Depends how it's cooked, and roo is usually served pink:

variants.label: Cooked right through
variants.why: Cooked through with no pink and served hot, roo is a green light and one of the leanest, most iron-rich meats going. Slow cooking keeps it tender.

variants.label: Served rare or medium-rare
variants.why: Roo is usually recommended rare so it stays tender, but pink meat carries the toxoplasmosis risk for now.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask for it well done, or slow-cook it so cooked through still means tender.
variants.swap: Kangaroo mince cooked right through in a rich bolognese.

foods.name: Turducken
foods.why: A bird in a bird in a bird is the stuffing problem three times over: the middle can stay undercooked while the outside looks ready. NSW Food Authority already reds stuffing cooked inside the bird.
foods.makeItGreen: Roast the birds and the stuffing as separate trays so everything cooks right through, then stack the plate.
foods.swap: A classic roast turkey with the stuffing baked in its own dish.

foods.name: Fried chicken, fresh and hot
foods.why: Fried until it is cooked right through and served hot, fried chicken is a green light, bucket and all. Eat it fresh; cold leftovers need a proper steaming reheat first.

foods.name: Hot dogs and frankfurts
foods.why: Depends whether it's steaming or straight from the pack:

variants.label: Heated until steaming hot
variants.why: Boiled, grilled or battered and fried, then served steaming, hot dogs and dagwood dogs are a green light. Listeria taps out at 74 degrees held for 2 minutes.

variants.label: Cold from the packet
variants.why: Frankfurts are pre-cooked then chilled, which makes them ready-to-eat cold meat, and cheerios off the party platter count too.
variants.makeItGreen: Simmer or grill them until they are steaming hot right through.
variants.swap: A hot dog fresh off the barbie, sauce and all.

foods.name: Corned beef and silverside
foods.why: Depends whether it's from your pot or the deli:

variants.label: Home-cooked silverside, served hot
variants.why: Simmered for hours and served hot with white sauce, corned silverside is thoroughly cooked. An old-school green light.

variants.label: Cold sliced corned beef
variants.why: Cold corned beef, from the deli or yesterday's silverside eaten cold from the fridge, counts as ready-to-eat cold meat.
variants.makeItGreen: Reheat it until steaming, or grill it into a hot corned beef and cheese toastie.
variants.swap: Hot silverside with white sauce, straight from the pot.

foods.name: Meatloaf, served hot
foods.why: Baked until cooked right through and served hot, meatloaf is a green light and a freezer-friendly legend. Cold slices from the fridge want a steaming reheat first.

foods.name: Canned smoked oysters and mussels
foods.why: Smoked seafood is usually a no, but the tin changes the answer. Canning heat-treats the lot, so smoked oysters and mussels from a can are a green light.

foods.name: Canned tuna, salmon and sardines
foods.why: Canning does all the safety work for you, and tinned fish is a brilliant omega-3 hit. A small tin of tuna counts as half a serve, so several tins a week is fine.

foods.name: Ceviche
foods.why: Citrus firms the fish up so it looks cooked, but that is chemistry, not heat, and the bugs never got the memo. Ceviche still counts as raw.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook the fish right through and serve it hot with the same lime, chilli and coriander over the top.
foods.swap: Hot grilled fish tacos with lime, coriander and plenty of avo.

foods.name: Fish and chips
foods.why: Straight out of the fryer and piping hot, battered fish is a green light. One thing worth asking at the counter: if the fish is flake, that is shark, and shark has a mercury cap.

foods.name: Flake (shark), swordfish and marlin
foods.why: Heads up: flake at the fish and chip shop IS shark. Shark, swordfish, broadbill and marlin carry the most mercury, so it is one serve a fortnight and no other fish that fortnight.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep it to one 150g serve a fortnight, and eat no other fish in that fortnight.
foods.swap: Ask the shop for snapper, whiting or flathead instead: same batter, same chips, no mercury cap.

split.note: Our two sources genuinely disagree on the limit for these fish, so here is both sides. Stricter wins, and that is the fortnight.

positions.label: Royal Women's
positions.says: One 150g serve a fortnight of shark, swordfish, broadbill or marlin, and no other fish in that fortnight.

positions.label: Monash IVF
positions.says: Once a week for these high mercury fish. That is the gentler reading of the two, so it is not the one we put on the badge.

foods.name: Freshly cooked fish, served hot
foods.why: Hot off the grill and flaking apart, cooked fish is the default good choice. Fish is actively encouraged here: 1 to 3 serves a week, a serve being about 150g.

foods.name: Freshly cooked prawns, lobster, crab and calamari
foods.why: Cooked fresh and served hot, the whole shellfish crew is yours. Heat is the entire trick, so tuck in while it is still steaming rather than saving it for later.

foods.name: Freshly made sushi with cooked fillings
foods.why: Rolled in front of you with cooked fillings and eaten straight away, sushi is a green light. Nothing raw, nothing smoked, and no time spent sitting in a fridge.

foods.name: Marinated mussels
foods.why: Marinated seafood from the deli fridge is ready to eat and has not been near heat since it was packed. Listeria is very comfortable in the cold.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook mussels fresh and eat them hot, straight out of the pot with the shells steaming.
foods.swap: A hot pot of steamed mussels in garlic and tomato, with bread for the sauce.

foods.name: Orange roughy and catfish
foods.why: Orange roughy (sometimes sold as sea perch) and catfish sit mid-table for mercury. One serve a week, with no other fish that week, keeps you comfortably inside the limit.
foods.makeItGreen: One 150g serve a week, and make it the only fish that week.
foods.swap: Snapper, barramundi, whiting or tinned tuna, none of which come with a weekly cap.

foods.name: Prawns
foods.why: Depends how they're served:

variants.label: Freshly cooked, served hot
variants.why: Hot garlic prawns, salt and pepper prawns, prawns off the barbecue: cooked fresh and eaten hot, they are a green light and a lovely iron hit.

variants.label: Cold and pre-cooked
variants.why: Cold cooked prawns may have been cooked hours ago, then chilled and handled since, which is listeria territory.
variants.makeItGreen: Reheat them right through until they are steaming, or order them hot off the pan in the first place.
variants.swap: Hot garlic prawns instead of the prawn cocktail, and you get the better version anyway.

variants.label: Raw
variants.why: Raw prawns in sashimi, ceviche or a marinade have not been cooked at all, so nothing has dealt with the bacteria.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook them until they turn opaque and are hot right through.
variants.swap: Cooked prawn nigiri made fresh, or a hot chilli prawn stir-fry.

foods.name: Pre-cooked cold prawns
foods.why: Sold ready-cooked and chilled, these may have been sitting around a while, and cold ready-to-eat seafood is listeria's favourite address. Heat is the fix.
foods.makeItGreen: Reheat them until they are steaming hot right through, or order them hot in the first place.
foods.swap: Hot garlic prawns, or a prawn stir-fry cooked until they curl and sizzle.

foods.name: Pre-made or store-bought sushi
foods.why: Even with cooked fillings, sushi that has been sitting in a fridge or a display case has had time for listeria to settle in. It is the sitting, not the filling.
foods.makeItGreen: Sushi made fresh in front of you with cooked fillings, eaten straight away, is a green light.
foods.swap: A hot teriyaki chicken don, or home-made cooked rolls with tinned tuna and avo.

foods.name: Raw oysters
foods.why: Raw oysters filter everything the water has to offer and nothing gets cooked out. Shellfish this raw waits until after the birth.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked hot right through, like oysters Kilpatrick bubbling out from under the grill, and they are back on.
foods.swap: Kilpatrick, oysters mornay, or a plate of hot salt and pepper squid.

foods.name: Salmon
foods.why: Depends how it's served:

variants.label: Cooked through, served hot
variants.why: Baked, grilled or pan-fried until it flakes, salmon is one of the best things on the menu. Fish is encouraged at 1 to 3 serves a week, and salmon is a low-mercury one.

variants.label: Smoked or raw
variants.why: Cold-smoked salmon, gravlax and raw salmon are ready-to-eat and chilled, which is exactly where listeria likes to sit.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook it right through in a hot dish and eat it steaming: a salmon and pasta bake, or smoked salmon stirred into a hot quiche.
variants.swap: Canned salmon with cream cheese on a toasted bagel gives you the same salty hit.

variants.label: Canned
variants.why: Canning heat-treats the lot, so tinned salmon is safe, cheap and a cracking omega-3 delivery system.

foods.name: Sashimi, raw sushi and poke
foods.why: Raw fish can carry listeria, one of the few bugs that keeps growing in a cold fridge. Sashimi, raw nigiri and poke are benched for the next few months.
foods.makeItGreen: Rolls made fresh in front of you with cooked fillings, like teriyaki chicken, tinned tuna or avocado, are back on the menu.
foods.swap: A cooked-roll sushi night at home, or hot garlic prawns with rice.

foods.name: Smoked salmon, smoked trout and gravlax
foods.why: Cold smoked fish is chilled, ready to eat and never actually cooked, which is exactly the setup listeria likes. Canned or cooked right through is a different story.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked right through in a hot dish, like a salmon and leek pasta bake straight from the oven, and it is a green light.
foods.swap: Canned salmon with cream cheese on a toasted bagel does the same job.

foods.name: Ling
foods.why: Ling is a mild, meaty white fish with no mercury cap, so cooked through and served hot it is an easy green light. Fish is encouraged here: 1 to 3 serves a week.

foods.name: Blue grenadier (hoki)
foods.why: Hoki, also sold as blue grenadier, is a low-mercury white fish. Cooked through and served hot it is green, and it is quietly the fish inside a lot of crumbed fillets and fish burgers.

foods.name: Basa
foods.why: Basa is a catfish, and catfish carries a once-a-week mercury cap, same as orange roughy. Farmed basa may well run milder, but the cap is the safe call, so one serve a week it is.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep it to one 150g serve a week with no other fish that week, or simply pick a fish without a cap.
foods.swap: Hoki, ling or whiting: the same flaky white fillet, no weekly limit.

foods.name: John dory
foods.why: John dory is a lovely low-mercury choice, cooked through and served hot. One menu trap: sea perch usually means orange roughy, which carries a once-a-week cap, so it pays to check which dory you are getting.

foods.name: Bream
foods.why: Grilled, baked or crispy-skinned in a pan, bream is a low-mercury local staple. Cooked through and served hot, it is a green light.

foods.name: Garfish
foods.why: Butterflied and lightly fried, garfish is a little treasure with no mercury cap. Cooked through and served hot, tuck in.

foods.name: Trevally
foods.why: Trevally is a low-mercury fish with no weekly cap, so cooked through and hot it is green. Raw trevally in sashimi is a different story and waits until after bub.

foods.name: Mahi mahi
foods.why: Mahi mahi is not on the mercury caution lists, so cooked through and served hot it is a green light within the usual 1 to 3 serves of fish a week.

foods.name: Kingfish
foods.why: Depends how it's served:

variants.label: Cooked through, served hot
variants.why: Cooked through and served hot, kingfish is a green light with no mercury cap. Grill it, bake it, glaze it.

variants.label: Sashimi, crudo or cured
variants.why: Raw kingfish is the menu's favourite sashimi, and raw fish waits until after bub, same as the rest of the sashimi list.
variants.makeItGreen: Cooked through is the flip: ask for it grilled instead.
variants.swap: Grilled kingfish, or cooked-through salmon.

foods.name: Fresh tuna steak
foods.why: Depends how it's cooked:

variants.label: Cooked through
variants.why: Tuna is not on the tight mercury lists, so a steak cooked right through sits with the everyday fish at 1 to 3 serves a week. A small tin even counts as half a serve.

variants.label: Seared rare
variants.why: Seared tuna with a pink, cool middle is mostly raw fish, and raw fish is where listeria hides.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask for it cooked through. Same crust, same dressing, none of the worry.
variants.swap: Canned tuna does the poke-style job at home with zero fuss.

foods.name: Fresh trout
foods.why: Baked or pan-fried until it flakes, fresh trout is a green light and a lovely omega-3 hit. It is the smoked trout from the fridge pack that is a no; cooked fresh trout is a yes.

foods.name: Grilled octopus
foods.why: Hot off the char-grill, octopus is a green light. The one to skip is the cold marinated octopus in the deli tub, which is ready-to-eat seafood that has been sitting chilled.

foods.name: Balmain bugs
foods.why: Grilled with garlic butter and served hot, balmain bugs are a green light, same as their lobster cousins. Cooked fresh and eaten hot is the whole trick.

foods.name: Pipis and vongole
foods.why: Steamed open in a hot pan and eaten straight away, pipis and vongole are green. Any that stay shut stay in the pot, and the cold marinated versions from the deli are a no.

foods.name: Oysters Kilpatrick and mornay
foods.why: This is the green face of oysters. Kilpatrick or mornay bubbling hot from under the grill means the oyster is properly cooked, and cooked hot oysters are back on the menu.

foods.name: Canned mackerel and herring
foods.why: The tin does the safety work: canned mackerel, herring and kipper fillets are green, just like tinned tuna, even the smoked ones. Cheap, shelf-stable, great omega-3s. Fridge them once opened.

foods.name: Fish roe and caviar
foods.why: Caviar, ikura, tobiko and their kin are cold, ready-to-eat seafood that never sees heat, which is exactly where listeria likes to sit. Same logic as the raw fish they usually top.
foods.makeItGreen: Roe cooked right through in a hot dish is fine. It is the cold spoonful on blinis and sushi that waits.
foods.swap: For the salty pop, try capers, or canned smoked oysters on a cracker.

foods.name: Seafood extender (surimi)
foods.why: Seafood sticks are cooked at the factory, but they are sold chilled and eaten cold in salads and cold rolls, which is cold ready-to-eat seafood territory. The sitting is the problem, not the stick.
foods.makeItGreen: Tossed through a hot stir-fry, laksa or fried rice and served steaming, it is fine.
foods.swap: Canned tuna or hot garlic prawns give the seafood hit without the fridge time.

foods.name: Whitebait
foods.why: Fried crisp and served hot, whitebait is a green light: tiny fish cooked right through. Eat them fresh from the fryer rather than cold off a buffet.

foods.name: Thai fish cakes
foods.why: Fried to order and served hot, Thai fish cakes are cooked right through, so they are a green light. The sweet chilli dipping sauce from a bottle is fine too.

foods.name: Tuna mornay and fish pie
foods.why: A hot baked fish dish is a double win: tinned tuna is already safe, and the oven heat sorts out the rest. Serve it bubbling, fridge leftovers fast and reheat until steaming.

foods.name: Marinara mix
foods.why: The mixed seafood bag is green once it is properly cooked: simmer it right through in a hot sauce until every piece is opaque and the dish is steaming. Undercooked pieces are the only trap.

foods.name: Salmon patties
foods.why: The tinned-salmon patty is a pregnancy all-star: canned salmon is safe, and pan-frying until golden and hot right through finishes the job. Calcium bonus if the soft bones go in too.

foods.name: Cakes and biscuits, baked
foods.why: Once it has had its time in the oven, the egg in the batter is cooked through. Cake, bikkies and banana bread are all clear. It is only the raw batter that is benched.

foods.name: Chocolate mousse
foods.why: Classic mousse gets its cloud from raw egg, whipped in and never cooked, so the restaurant and homemade ones are out for now.
foods.makeItGreen: A mousse made without raw egg, like a cooked-custard or melted-chocolate-and-cream one, is fine. Worth asking the kitchen.
foods.swap: Chocolate custard, a warm self-saucing pudding, or ice cream from a tub.

foods.name: Eggnog
foods.why: Traditional nog is raw egg whisked into cream, and there is usually a slug of brandy in there too. Two good reasons to sit this one out at Chrissy.
foods.makeItGreen: A nog cooked custard-style until it thickens, with the booze left out, is fine.
foods.swap: Warm milk with nutmeg and vanilla, or shop-bought custard poured over ice.

foods.name: Eggs
foods.why: Depends how they're cooked:

variants.label: Cooked firm, yolk set
variants.why: Hard-boiled, firm scrambled, set omelette or fried until the yolk thickens. Cooked firm, eggs are a straight yes and a brilliant protein hit.

variants.label: Runny, poached or soft-boiled
variants.why: A yolk that still runs has not got hot enough to see off salmonella.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask for the yolks cooked firm, or give it another minute in the pan. Cafes do it all day without blinking.
variants.swap: Firm-yolk fried eggs on smashed avo, or a slice of set frittata.

variants.label: Raw in a sauce or dessert
variants.why: Cafe mayo, house aioli, hollandaise, mousse and tiramisu all use the egg raw.
variants.makeItGreen: Jar mayonnaise and shelf-stable commercial aioli are made with pasteurised egg, so those are all clear.
variants.swap: Pavlova, quiche or a chocolate brownie: baked egg desserts you can dive straight into.

variants.label: Baked into cakes, quiche or pav
variants.why: Baked is cooked. Cakes, bikkies, quiche and pavlova are all fine, so the national treasure stays intact.

foods.name: Eggs cooked firm
foods.why: Cooked until the white sets and the yolk thickens, eggs are a straight yes and a cracking protein hit. Hard-boiled, firm scrambled, set omelette or frittata: all yours.

foods.name: Eggs with cracked shells
foods.why: A cracked shell lets bacteria wander straight in, so that one goes in the bin, not the pan. The rest of the carton is still perfectly good.
foods.swap: Any egg with a clean, unbroken shell, cooked until the yolk is firm.

foods.name: Hollandaise and béarnaise
foods.why: Both sauces are barely-warmed raw egg yolk, which puts them in the raw-egg camp. This is the classic eggs benny trap, and it is not on you for loving it.
foods.makeItGreen: Ordered with firm-cooked eggs and the sauce left off, brunch is back on.
foods.swap: Smashed avo for the creamy bit, or lemon and melted butter over your greens.

foods.name: Homemade or cafe mayonnaise and aioli
foods.why: Whipped up fresh at home or in a cafe kitchen, mayo and aioli are raw egg with a fancy name, so salmonella is the risk. The jar version has none of that drama.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask whether the mayo or aioli came out of a jar or a commercial bottle. If it did, you are all good.
foods.swap: Jar mayonnaise, or lemon juice and olive oil on the side.

foods.name: Jar mayonnaise and commercial aioli
foods.why: Mayo from a jar or a squeezy bottle is made with pasteurised egg, so it is a green light on your sanga. Keep it in the fridge once open and follow the label.

foods.name: Licking the cake batter
foods.why: The cruellest rule on the list: raw batter means raw egg. The bowl and the beaters will keep for a few months, and the baked version is completely yours.
foods.makeItGreen: Bake it first. Cooked cake, bikkies and brownies are completely fine.
foods.swap: Ten minutes of patience and a warm slice straight from the oven.

foods.name: Mayonnaise
foods.why: Depends where it came from:

variants.label: From a jar or squeezy bottle
variants.why: Commercial mayonnaise and shelf-stable aioli are made with pasteurised egg. Keep it in the fridge once opened and go by the label.

variants.label: Homemade or cafe-made
variants.why: House mayo and house aioli are usually built on raw egg, which brings salmonella along for the ride.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask the magic question: is the mayo from a jar? Most kitchens will happily tell you, and most of them use jar mayo anyway.
variants.swap: Jar mayo, or smashed avo for the same creamy, tangy hit.

variants.label: In a shop-made salad or sandwich
variants.why: Deli coleslaw, potato salad and pre-made sandwiches carry the sitting-time risk on top of the raw-egg question.
variants.makeItGreen: Make it at home with jar mayo and eat it the same day, and it is a green light.
variants.swap: A fresh toastie made in front of you, hot off the press.

foods.name: Pavlova
foods.why: Baked meringue is cooked meringue, so the pav is safe as houses. Top it with cream and fruit you cut at home and enjoy the lot. National treasure: intact.

foods.name: Quiche
foods.why: Quiche bakes until the egg custard sets, and baked means cooked, so it is a yes. With leftovers, keep them cold, eat them within a day and reheat until steaming.

foods.name: Restaurant Caesar salad
foods.why: The traditional dressing is raw egg yolk, so the restaurant version is out for now. The cold sliced chicken that often comes with it is not helping either.
foods.makeItGreen: Made at home with jar mayo, hot grilled chicken and hot crispy bacon, Caesar is back on the menu.
foods.swap: A home Caesar with jar-mayo dressing, hot chicken and a snowstorm of parmesan.

foods.name: Runny, poached or soft-boiled eggs
foods.why: A runny yolk can carry salmonella, so this one is benched for a few months. Ask for the yolks cooked firm and the rest of the brekkie is all yours.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for the yolks cooked firm: hard-poached, over hard, or fried until the yolk sets. Cafes do it all day without blinking.
foods.swap: A slice of set frittata, or firm-yolk fried eggs on smashed avo.

foods.name: Tiramisu
foods.why: The creamy layers are mascarpone whipped with raw egg, so the classic build is a no for now. The coffee and cocoa were never the problem.
foods.makeItGreen: An egg-free tiramisu, mascarpone and cream only, is fine. Easy to ask about, easy to make that way at home.
foods.swap: Affogato with tub ice cream and a decaf shot, or a slice of coffee cake.

foods.name: Shakshuka
foods.why: Depends how long the eggs get under the lid:

variants.label: Yolks cooked until set
variants.why: Eggs baked in that rich tomato sauce until the yolks are firm are cooked eggs, full stop. A brilliant brekkie, and the feta on top gets cooked right along with it.

variants.label: Yolks still runny
variants.why: Most cafes pull shakshuka while the yolks are still soft, and a runny yolk has not got hot enough to see off salmonella.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask for the eggs well set. A few extra minutes under the lid is all it takes, and the sauce is none the wiser.
variants.swap: Firm-yolk fried eggs with a side of tomato relish, or a slice of set frittata.

foods.name: Carbonara
foods.why: Depends how the sauce is made:

variants.label: Classic, egg tossed through off the heat
variants.why: The silky classic is raw egg stirred through hot pasta with the pan off the heat. The pasta warms the egg but does not cook it, so the raw-egg rule benches it for now.
variants.makeItGreen: Ask if the sauce is cream-based or cooked right through until steaming. Plenty of Aussie kitchens make it with cream anyway, so it is an easy question.
variants.swap: A creamy boscaiola, bacon and mushroom in real cream, scratches the exact same itch.

variants.label: Cream-based, or cooked until piping hot
variants.why: A carbonara built on cream has no raw egg to worry about, and a sauce cooked through on the heat until it is steaming has done the egg properly.

foods.name: Creme brulee
foods.why: A brulee is custard baked gently until it sets, so the egg is cooked long before the blowtorch shows up. The crackly top is just sugar. Order away.

foods.name: Creme caramel and flan
foods.why: Creme caramel is baked custard through and through, cooked in the oven until it sets, and baked means cooked. The caramel is just sugar. All yours.

foods.name: Lemon curd
foods.why: Curd is cooked until it thickens, and that thickening is the egg cooking: jar lemon butter and homemade are both fine. Baked lemon meringue pie gets the nod; if the cafe torches the meringue instead, ask.

foods.name: Macarons
foods.why: Macaron shells are baked meringue, and baked meringue is cooked, so these fancy little numbers are a yes. Coconut macaroons and meringue kisses ride the same rule: out of the oven, all good.

foods.name: Royal icing
foods.why: Depends what the icing is made from:

variants.label: Classic, made with raw egg white
variants.why: Traditional royal icing is raw egg white whipped with sugar and never cooked, so it sits in the raw-egg camp right next to the cake batter.
variants.makeItGreen: Make it with meringue powder or pasteurised carton egg white and it is exactly the same icing, minus the worry.
variants.swap: A simple glace icing, just icing sugar and water, sets hard too.

variants.label: Meringue powder or ready-made
variants.why: Icing made from meringue powder, pasteurised egg white or a supermarket packet has no raw egg in it. Pipe away.

foods.name: Quail eggs
foods.why: Depends how they're cooked, same rules as chook eggs:

variants.label: Cooked firm
variants.why: Tiny eggs, same deal: boiled or fried until the yolk sets and they are a lovely little protein hit.

variants.label: Runny or raw
variants.why: A soft-centred quail egg, or a raw one perched on top of a dish, carries the same salmonella risk as any runny egg.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook them through until the yolks are firm. They are small, so it only takes a minute or two.
variants.swap: A firm-boiled chook egg does the same job with less fiddling.

foods.name: Duck eggs
foods.why: Depends how they're cooked, same rules as chook eggs:

variants.label: Cooked firm
variants.why: Bigger and richer than chook eggs, but the same rule applies: cooked until the white is set and the yolk is firm, they are a yes.

variants.label: Runny or soft
variants.why: Duck eggs are big, so the middle takes longer to cook than you would think. A runny yolk is the same salmonella story as any egg.
variants.makeItGreen: Give them a couple of extra minutes in the pan so the yolk sets right through.
variants.swap: Firm-cooked chook eggs if you want a quicker, more forgiving cook.

foods.name: Devilled and curried eggs
foods.why: Depends whose mayo is in the mix:

variants.label: Made at home with jar mayo, eaten fresh
variants.why: The egg is hard-boiled and the jar mayo is pasteurised, so a fresh batch made at home is a green light.

variants.label: Party platter or cafe-made
variants.why: House-made mayo means raw egg, and platter eggs can sit out for hours, which stacks the sitting-time problem on top.
variants.makeItGreen: Make them yourself with jar mayo and eat them the same day.
variants.swap: A fresh hard-boiled egg with a dollop of jar mayo and a dust of curry powder.

foods.name: Scotch eggs
foods.why: Depends how it reaches you:

variants.label: Hot and freshly cooked through
variants.why: A scotch egg fried or baked until the sausage layer is cooked through around a hard-boiled egg is cooked food served hot. Lovely.

variants.label: Cold from the deli or servo fridge
variants.why: Sitting cold in a cabinet puts it in refrigerated ready-to-eat territory, which is where listeria likes to lurk.
variants.makeItGreen: Reheat it until it is steaming hot right through and it is back on the menu.
variants.swap: A hot sausage roll straight out of the oven.

foods.name: Egg salad sandwich
foods.why: Depends where it was made:

variants.label: Made at home with jar mayo, eaten fresh
variants.why: Hard-boiled egg plus pasteurised jar mayo, made and eaten the same day, is a straight yes and a great cheap lunch.

variants.label: Pre-made from a fridge cabinet
variants.why: Shop sandwiches that sit refrigerated are a listeria risk whatever the filling, and you cannot tell whose mayo is hiding inside.
variants.makeItGreen: Order one made fresh in front of you and ask for mayo from the jar or squeezy bottle.
variants.swap: A toasted egg sanga, hot off the press.

foods.name: Avocado
foods.why: Smashed, sliced or scooped straight out of the skin, avo is a green light. Rinse the skin before you cut it so the knife stays clean on the way in.

foods.name: Cafe and juice-bar juices and smoothies
foods.why: Two problems in the one cup: fruit that was cut hours ago, and juicers and blenders that are genuinely hard to clean properly.
foods.makeItGreen: Blend it at home from washed whole fruit and drink it straight away, and it is a green light.
foods.swap: A bottled pasteurised juice from the fridge aisle, or a smoothie out of your own blender.

foods.name: Canned and dried fruit
foods.why: Sealed tins and dried fruit are a yes any day. Dried apricots and prunes are quietly brilliant for iron and for keeping things moving along.

foods.name: Canned vegetables
foods.why: Straight off the shelf and good to go. Once the tin is open, follow the storage note on the label and tip the leftovers into a container in the fridge.

foods.name: Cooked mushrooms
foods.why: Wash them, cook them hot, enjoy them. Grilled mushies on the big brekky are a green light, with one exception: enoki, which has its own card.

foods.name: Cooked vegetables
foods.why: Wash them, cook them, eat them: veg is where a lot of the good stuff lives. Roasted, steamed or stir fried, the whole lot is a green light.

foods.name: Enoki mushrooms
foods.why: Enoki has been behind listeria outbreaks here in Australia, so raw or barely wilted in a hot pot it is a no for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked right through and piping hot, stir fried or simmered in a soup for a few minutes, enoki is fine.
foods.swap: Button or swiss brown mushrooms, cooked hot in the pan, do the same job in a stir fry.

foods.name: Fresh fruit, washed
foods.why: Bananas, apples, berries, mango: all a straight yes. Give fruit a wash under the tap first, skin and all, even the bits you are not going to eat.

foods.name: Fresh herbs, washed
foods.why: Give them a good rinse and scatter away. Basil, coriander, parsley and mint are all a green light, straight from the bunch onto the plate.

foods.name: Frozen fruit
foods.why: Frozen fruit is a yes. Imported frozen berries have been recalled before, so the extra-cautious move is to cook them first or pick Australian grown.

split.note: The advice genuinely splits a little here, so both sides are below. The verdict stays green either way.

positions.label: Royal Women's
positions.says: Frozen fruit is safe.

positions.label: The recall history
positions.says: Imported frozen berries have been recalled in Australia before. The extra-careful move is to cook them first, or pick Australian grown. Your call, and both are reasonable.

foods.name: Frozen vegetables
foods.why: Frozen veg is a yes once it is cooked. NSW Food Authority asks you not to eat it straight from the packet, so give it a proper hot cook first.

foods.name: Fruit cut at home
foods.why: You control the knife, the board and the clock, so fruit you wash and cut yourself is a green light. Keep it in the fridge and eat it the same day.

foods.name: Juice and smoothies made at home
foods.why: You are the juice bar now: washed whole fruit, your own clean blender, drunk straight away. That is the entire rule, and it is a yes.

foods.name: Mushrooms
foods.why: Depends on the type, and how cooked:

variants.label: Cooked mushrooms
variants.why: Grilled, roasted or fried button, cup, Swiss brown, portobello or field mushies are a straight yes, and a big brekkie without them is a sadder plate.

variants.label: Raw and washed, in a home salad
variants.why: Common mushrooms raw are washed-veg territory: give them a good rinse, make the salad yourself and eat it fresh.

variants.label: Enoki, raw or lightly cooked
variants.why: Enoki are a known listeria carrier and have been behind Australian recalls, so the thin raw ones on top of a bowl are out.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook them right through until they are hot and soft, simmered into a soup, hot pot or stir-fry.
variants.swap: Sliced Swiss browns or shiitake, cooked hot, for the same earthy flavour.

foods.name: Potatoes
foods.why: Spuds are a yes in every form you can cook them: mashed, roasted, baked or boiled. Give the skin a scrub first if the jacket is coming along too.

foods.name: Raw sprouts
foods.why: NSW Food Authority benches every kind raw or lightly cooked, alfalfa through to mung. Seeds sprout in warm damp conditions, and bacteria love that too.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked properly hot right through, tossed into a stir fry or a soup until they go soft, sprouts are back on.
foods.swap: Grated carrot, cucumber ribbons or shredded cabbage give you the same crunch in a sandwich.

foods.name: Rockmelon
foods.why: Rockmelon's rough rind can trap bacteria that the knife drags through the flesh, and one of our sources says skip it entirely. Stricter wins, so it is benched for now.
foods.swap: Watermelon, honeydew or mango, washed and cut at home, gives you the same sweet juicy hit.

split.note: Two of our sources genuinely disagree on this one, so here is both sides. Stricter wins, which is why it stays benched for now.

positions.label: Royal Women's
positions.says: A whole rockmelon, washed well and cut at home, is allowed. The real danger zone is pre-cut melon from a shop, where listeria loves to settle.

positions.label: NSW Food Authority
positions.says: Do not eat rockmelon at all while pregnant. The rough rind traps bacteria that can be carried through the flesh when it is cut.

foods.name: Salad bars and pre-packaged salads
foods.why: Someone else washed it, someone else cut it, and nobody can tell you how long it has been sitting out. A sneeze guard does not stop listeria.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for it made fresh in front of you, or build the very same salad at home.
foods.swap: A home-made garden salad, or hot cooked veg on the side instead.

foods.name: Salad made fresh at home
foods.why: Lettuce help: wash everything well, build it fresh and eat it soon after. The only thing to leave out is raw sprouts, which have their own card.

foods.name: Shop fruit salad
foods.why: Pre-cut fruit plus an unknown amount of sitting time is exactly the combination listeria likes. Not this one for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Make it at home from washed whole fruit and eat it the same day.
foods.swap: Home-cut fruit salad with a spoon of yoghurt and a drizzle of honey on top.

foods.name: Store-bought pre-cut fruit
foods.why: Once fruit is cut it sits wet and cool for hours, which is listeria weather. Pre-cut melon is the riskiest of the lot.
foods.makeItGreen: Buy it whole, wash the skin and cut it yourself at home. Same fruit, no worries.
foods.swap: A whole banana, apple or mandarin off the same shelf: nature's own packaging.

foods.name: Watermelon and honeydew
foods.why: The rough-rind worry is rockmelon's alone. Smooth-skinned melons, washed whole and cut at home, are green. Shop pre-cut melon of any kind is a no, and that one has its own card.

foods.name: Strawberries, washed
foods.why: Strawberries are a washed-fruit yes. Give them a good rinse under running water just before eating, hulls still on, then go for it.

foods.name: Blueberries and raspberries
foods.why: Fresh blueberries, raspberries and blackberries are green once they have had a rinse. Frozen berries have their own card with one extra honesty note.

foods.name: Mangoes
foods.why: Mango season is all yours. Wash the skin before you cut, so the knife stays clean on the way through, and cheeks cut at home are a green light.

foods.name: Grapes and cherries
foods.why: Grapes and cherries are washed-fruit green. Rinse the whole bunch well under the tap and graze away. Grapes you freeze yourself at home count too.

foods.name: Kiwifruit
foods.why: Green, gold, or cut in half and eaten with a spoon: kiwifruit is a washed-fruit yes. Rinse the outside first, even though nobody is eating the fuzz.

foods.name: Apples and pears
foods.why: Washed whole apples and pears are about as green as food gets. A crisp pink lady or a ripe packham straight from the fruit bowl is a perfect snack.

foods.name: Citrus fruit
foods.why: Oranges, mandarins, lemons, limes and grapefruit are whole washed fruit: a straight yes. Peel-and-eat fruit is nature's own snack packaging.

foods.name: Papaya
foods.why: Ripe papaya, washed whole and cut at home, is washed-fruit green. The green papaya salad question is about shop prep and sitting time, not the fruit itself.

foods.name: Pomegranate
foods.why: A whole pomegranate you wash and crack open at home is washed-fruit green. Tubs of ready-podded arils sit in pre-cut territory, so pod your own.

foods.name: Fresh figs
foods.why: Fresh figs are washed-fruit green. A gentle rinse of the skin, then eat them fresh while they are perfect, because figs never wait around for anyone.

foods.name: Stone fruit
foods.why: Peaches, nectarines, plums and apricots are whole washed fruit: green all summer long. A quick rinse under the tap first, fuzz and all.

foods.name: Bagged salad leaves
foods.why: Pre-packaged salads are on the bench list. Washed-and-ready leaves can pick up listeria between the factory and your fridge, and another rinse at home cannot undo that.
foods.makeItGreen: Buy whole heads or bunches instead and wash the leaves yourself just before eating.
foods.swap: A salad built at home from whole washed veg, or hot cooked greens on the side.

foods.name: Spinach
foods.why: Depends on bunch, bag or freezer:

variants.label: Bunch spinach or silverbeet, washed at home
variants.why: Wash it well and it is yours: fresh in a home salad, wilted into pasta or cooked right down. Green.

variants.label: Bagged pre-washed baby spinach
variants.why: Pre-packaged salad leaves are benched: the bag can carry listeria from the factory and a rinse at home cannot re-wash it clean.
variants.makeItGreen: Buy the bunch or loose leaves and wash them yourself, or cook the bagged stuff hot right through.
variants.swap: A bunch of English spinach, washed at the sink.

variants.label: Frozen spinach, cooked
variants.why: Fine once it is properly cooked. NSW Food Authority just asks that frozen veg never goes in straight from the packet.

foods.name: Kale
foods.why: Depends on bunch or bag:

variants.label: A whole bunch, washed at home
variants.why: Washed well and massaged into a salad, baked into chips or cooked hot, bunch kale is a green light.

variants.label: Bagged pre-washed kale or kale salad mix
variants.why: Same rule as every pre-washed bag: pre-packaged salad leaves are benched because a home rinse cannot undo factory contamination.
variants.makeItGreen: Buy the bunch and wash it yourself, or cook the bagged kale hot right through.
variants.swap: A bunch of cavolo nero from the veg aisle, washed at home.

foods.name: Cos and iceberg lettuce
foods.why: A whole head you wash and pull apart at home is a green light. It is the pre-washed bags and the salad bars that are benched, and they each have their own card.

foods.name: Bagged coleslaw mix
foods.why: A bag of shredded slaw is a pre-packaged salad in party clothes: cut a long time ago, impossible to re-wash properly, and benched for the same reason as bagged leaves.
foods.makeItGreen: Shred cabbage and carrot at home and dress it with jar mayo. Five minutes, all green.
foods.swap: A crunchy home-made slaw, or grated carrot and cucumber ribbons.

foods.name: Kimchi
foods.why: Depends on the jar, and on the heat:

variants.label: Pasteurised jar from the supermarket shelf
variants.why: A shelf-stable pasteurised jar follows the canned-and-bottled rule: green. Into the fridge once opened, label rules apply.

variants.label: Fresh refrigerated kimchi, eaten raw
variants.why: Live unpasteurised kimchi is a raw ferment, the same family as the fermented drinks on the bench, so raw is a skip for now.
variants.makeItGreen: Cook it into the dish: kimchi fried rice, a bubbling jjigae or a kimchi pancake, served hot.
variants.swap: A pasteurised jar from the shelf, or quick-pickled cucumber made at home.

variants.label: Cooked hot into a dish
variants.why: Heat sorts it out. Kimchi fried rice or a simmering kimchi stew, served steaming, is a green light.

foods.name: Sauerkraut
foods.why: Depends on the jar:

variants.label: Pasteurised jar or can from the shelf
variants.why: Shelf-stable kraut is cooked in the canning, so the canned-and-bottled rule makes it green. Fridge and label rules after opening.

variants.label: Raw refrigerated kraut, the live-culture kind
variants.why: Raw live-culture kraut is the same raw-ferment family as the benched fermented drinks, so it sits out for now. Heat or pasteurisation flips it.
variants.makeItGreen: Heat it right through on the hot dog or in the pan, or choose the pasteurised jar instead.
variants.swap: Pasteurised jar sauerkraut, or a squeeze of pickle from a sealed jar.

foods.name: Olives from a jar
foods.why: Olives from a sealed jar or tin are green: the canned-and-bottled rule at work. Once it is open, keep the jar in the fridge and follow the label.

foods.name: Olive bar and deli antipasto
foods.why: The deli antipasto bar is salad-bar territory: open tubs, shared spoons and no way to know how long anything has been sitting there. Not this one for now.
foods.makeItGreen: The very same olives and marinated veg from a sealed jar on the shelf are green.
foods.swap: Jar kalamatas and jar sun-dried tomatoes, opened fresh at home.

foods.name: Sun-dried tomatoes
foods.why: Depends on jar or deli tub:

variants.label: Sealed jar in oil, from the shelf
variants.why: Bottled and shelf-stable follows the canned-and-bottled rule: green. Fridge and label rules once the jar is open.

variants.label: Loose from the deli tub or antipasto bar
variants.why: Open deli tubs are refrigerated ready-to-eat food with an unknown clock, the same reason the salad bar is benched.
variants.makeItGreen: Pick up a sealed jar from the shelf instead: same tomatoes, known history.
variants.swap: Roasted cherry tomatoes made hot at home.

foods.name: Microgreens
foods.why: Microgreens are grown warm and damp, exactly like sprouts, and raw sprouts are benched. Same conditions, same call: skip them raw for now.
foods.makeItGreen: Cooked hot right through, wilted into a stir fry or dropped into a simmering soup, they are fine.
foods.swap: Washed fresh herbs give the plate the same fancy-garnish lift.

foods.name: Wheatgrass shots
foods.why: A juice-bar wheatgrass shot runs straight into the juice-bar rule: hard-to-clean machines and produce juiced who-knows-when. The shot is benched, not the grass.
foods.makeItGreen: Grown and juiced at home, washed well and drunk straight away, the home-juice rule applies.
foods.swap: A bottled pasteurised green juice from the fridge aisle.

foods.name: Garlic and ginger
foods.why: Both green. Wash, peel, chop and cook away. Fresh ginger grated into your cooking is a quiet favourite on queasy days, and jar minced versions follow the bottled rule.

foods.name: 0.0% beers and zero-alcohol drinks
foods.why: In Australia a drink labelled 0.0 can still legally hold up to 0.5% alcohol. Plenty of people are comfortable with that, and it is a great one to raise at your next appointment.
foods.makeItGreen: Brands that state 0.0% and confirm no detectable alcohol are the safest pick here, and your midwife's take is the one that counts.
foods.swap: Soda water with lime and frozen berries in a proper glass, or a pasteurised juice spritz.

split.note: This is a genuine judgement call. The sheets never rule on zero beers themselves, so here is both sides.

positions.label: Royal Women's
positions.says: There is no safe amount of alcohol in pregnancy, no exceptions.

positions.label: The label fine print
positions.says: A drink labelled 0.0 can still legally hold up to 0.5% alcohol in Australia. Plenty of people are comfortable with that, which is why this is a midwife chat rather than a hard no.

foods.name: Alcohol
foods.why: No known safe amount in pregnancy, so it sits out the next few months. A splash cooked into a long-simmered sauce is one for your care team to call.
foods.swap: Sparkling water, lime and frozen berries in the good glass, or soda with a splash of pasteurised juice and a fat wedge of orange.

foods.name: Artificial sweeteners
foods.why: Fine in moderation, and that really is the whole story. The sweeteners approved for Australian food and drink are safe, there is just no need to go overboard.
foods.makeItGreen: In normal everyday amounts they are a green light.

foods.name: Coffee
foods.why: Caffeine has a daily cap of 200mg from everything combined. That is roughly 1 to 2 espresso-based coffees, or about 3 cups of instant.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep the whole day under 200mg and your coffee is a green light. The trick is counting the teas and colas in the same tally.
foods.swap: A decaf flat white, or warm milk with cinnamon when the budget is spent.

foods.name: Cola
foods.why: Cola carries caffeine, so it lands in the same 200mg daily cap: about 4 to 5 cans fits, shared with your coffees and teas.
foods.makeItGreen: Inside the day's 200mg caffeine total, cola is fine. Caffeine-free versions do not touch the tally at all.
foods.swap: Sparkling water with a big wedge of lime, or a lemonade if it is the fizz you are chasing.

foods.name: Decaf coffee
foods.why: Basically a free hug. Near enough to no caffeine, so it sits outside the daily budget and the 4pm one is entirely yours.

foods.name: Energy drinks
foods.why: Energy drinks stack caffeine with guarana and other stimulants, which blows past the 200mg daily cap quickly. Off the menu for now.
foods.swap: A cold brew that fits inside your caffeine budget, or an icy sparkling water when it is the cold hit you are after.

foods.name: Herbal tea
foods.why: A couple of cups a day of the common flavours, like ginger or peppermint, is the usual advice. Medicinal and slimming blends are a different beast entirely.
foods.makeItGreen: Stick to everyday flavours like ginger, peppermint and chamomile, keep it to a couple of cups, and run any medicinal blend past your midwife first.
foods.swap: Hot water with fresh lemon and a slice of ginger, or a decaf brew.

split.note: The sheets do not fully settle herbal tea, so this one is a judgement call. Here is both sides.

positions.label: The source sheets
positions.says: None of our pregnancy sheets sets a firm herbal tea rule. The usual advice is a couple of cups a day of the common flavours, like ginger or peppermint.

positions.label: Our call
positions.says: Yellow. Everyday flavours in sensible amounts look fine, but medicinal and slimming blends are untested territory, so those go to your midwife first.

foods.name: Home-made smoothies
foods.why: Your blender, your rules. Pasteurised milk or yoghurt plus washed fruit, blitzed and drunk straight away, is a green light every single time.

foods.name: Hot chocolate
foods.why: A hot choc counts toward the 200mg caffeine budget, but it is one of the lightest hitters going. Roughly 4 to 5 cups fits in a day.
foods.makeItGreen: Inside the day's 200mg caffeine total, it is a green light. Made on pasteurised milk at home, it is one of the easy ones.
foods.swap: Warm milk with cinnamon or vanilla: no caffeine, same cosy.

foods.name: Kombucha, kefir and ginger beer
foods.why: Fermented drinks are brewed with live cultures, so they carry a contamination risk plus a little leftover alcohol. NSW Food Authority says park them for now.
foods.swap: Dry ginger ale over ice for the same spicy fizz, or a fresh ginger tea if it is the tummy-settling you are after.

foods.name: Pasteurised bottled juice
foods.why: Pasteurised is the magic word. The bottled and carton stuff has already been heat-treated on your behalf, so pour a big one.

foods.name: Raw milk as a drink
foods.why: Without pasteurisation, listeria and friends stay right where they are in the bottle. This is the one dairy rule with no wiggle room in it.
foods.makeItGreen: Pasteurised milk, including UHT and long life, is a green light and tastes the same in your coffee.
foods.swap: Any pasteurised milk from the fridge aisle, dairy or otherwise.

foods.name: Soft drinks and sugary drinks
foods.why: Nothing unsafe here, it is just sometimes-food territory: lots of sugar and not much else. Save them for when you genuinely fancy one.
foods.makeItGreen: Treated as a sometimes drink rather than the daily one, there is nothing to worry about.
foods.swap: Sparkling water with fruit in it, or pasteurised juice topped up with soda water.

foods.name: Tea
foods.why: Tea draws on the same 200mg daily caffeine budget as coffee. Around 4 to 5 cups fits inside it, as long as coffee is not also on the tally.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep the day's caffeine total under 200mg and your cuppa is all clear.
foods.swap: A decaf brew, or hot water with lemon when the tally is nearly full.

foods.name: Water and sparkling water
foods.why: The GOAT of pregnancy drinks. Staying hydrated helps with just about everything, and the bubbly kind counts exactly the same as the still kind.

foods.name: Iced latte
foods.why: Same coffee, just colder. An iced latte draws on the exact same 200mg daily caffeine budget as the hot version, and the milk and ice are completely fine.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep the whole day under 200mg of caffeine and it is a green light. A decaf iced latte does not touch the tally at all.

foods.name: Affogato
foods.why: One espresso shot poured over tub ice cream. The shot counts toward your 200mg caffeine day, and tub ice cream is the safe kind, so this is a budget question, not a safety one.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for it decaf and it is a straight green. Either way, check the ice cream is scooped from a tub, not the soft-serve machine.

foods.name: Babycino
foods.why: Warm milk froth in a tiny cup, sometimes with a marshmallow on the side. No coffee, no caffeine, no worries. Order one and enjoy the cuteness rehearsal.

foods.name: Matcha
foods.why: Matcha counts toward the 200mg caffeine day, and because you drink the whole powdered leaf it packs more than a regular cup of green tea. One matcha latte a day fits the budget easily.
foods.makeItGreen: Keep the day's caffeine total under 200mg, counting your coffees and teas in the same tally, and matcha is all clear.
foods.swap: A turmeric latte brings the same golden-hour cafe energy with zero caffeine.

foods.name: Bubble tea
